A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same SIL-C research work, with complete 40-page main texts, references, Appendices A-D and checklists. Text extraction and rendered-page comparison establish reliable correspondence throughout.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulation experiments on Franka Kitchen and multi-stage Meta-World, including compatibility, few-shot learning, robustness and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original SIL-C simulation results on both environments, including the main comparisons, ablations and additional experiments in Appendices C-D.

M1.justification: The bilateral interface, skill validation and hooking, training objectives and update algorithms remain unchanged. Element-wise subtask memory already appears in Appendix D.2; the new Table 2 note documents its use in existing sparse-demonstration settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Franka Kitchen and multi-stage Meta-World datasets, Emergent/Explicit SIL scenarios, and existing few-shot and noisy-observation evaluations.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in corresponding experiments, including BUDS and PTGM configurations, Skill-prototypes, Instructions, and joint/multitask comparisons in the main text and Appendix C.

E3.justification: The data streams, demonstration budgets, sampling ratios, metrics and evaluation procedures are retained. The new prototype-handling note and decoder configuration fields disclose details for existing experiments; they do not establish revisions to previously specified experimental settings.

E4.justification: The interface ablations, phase-order tests, noise robustness, resolution sensitivity, memory-representation comparisons, distance metrics, threshold analysis and timing analysis remain unchanged in Section 6 and Appendices C-D.

E5.justification: Appendix B.6 retains four random seeds, reporting means and standard deviations, and three evaluations averaged per task. Timing variance reporting and other uncertainty information are also unchanged.

E6.justification: Numerical results and qualitative findings are unchanged throughout. For example, Table 2 retains SIL-C's 46.4 ± 5.7% BwSC AUC and PTGM's 23.5 ± 2.2% under one-shot, 20% transition sampling.

T1.justification: The MDP/SIL formulation, prototype-distance and interface equations, metric definitions in Appendix B.4, and memory/computation derivations in Appendix D.6 are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: maintaining forward and backward skill-policy compatibility through a bilateral lazy learning interface without downstream policy retraining or structural adaptation.

C2.justification: Interpretations of compatibility, sparse-supervision performance and noise resilience are unchanged. Section 7 retains the same applicability qualifications concerning simulation, state representations and clustering under more diverse skill distributions.

D1.justification: Table 2 newly specifies that SIL-C treats each sampled transition as an individual subtask prototype at 50% and 20% sampling. Table 11 adds a deterministic inference sampler with no added noise and a LoRA learning rate of 1×10^-4, alongside the retained default rate of 2×10^-5. These are limited reproducibility disclosures.

R1.justification: The cited works, reference list and positioning relative to skill incremental learning, continual model updates and lazy learning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The affiliation drops the leading 'The' from University of Texas at Austin, and Table 2 gains a short explanatory sentence. The narrative and section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 2's expanded caption shifts nearby content. Table 11 adds two configuration rows and uses smaller, more compact typography. The hardware list reflows across pages 25-26; all figures and tables are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 reduces reproducibility ambiguities by specifying the sparse-demonstration prototype rule and decoder inference/LoRA settings in Tables 2 and 11. These useful disclosures outweigh the modest readability cost of Table 11's smaller type. The gain is limited because the scientific claims and supporting experimental evidence remain unchanged.
